It raises the threshold to **-45 mV**. Here's why.

The drug is **shifting the voltage dependence of inactivation** to more negative potentials. Normally, sodium channels inactivate around -55 mV. If you shift that curve leftward, they now inactivate at **-65 mV** instead. That means at a resting potential of -70 mV, more channels are already inactivated before the cell even fires. The cell needs a **stronger depolarizing stimulus** to reach threshold because fewer excitable channels remain.

So the threshold itself doesn't move. What moves is the **availability of channels to open**. The cell becomes harder to excite — that is the **mechanism of use-dependent blockade** in ischemic tissue.

Alright. Let's use a door analogy.

Picture a sodium channel as a door with two locks: an **activation lock** (opens when voltage hits -55 mV) and an **inactivation lock** (slams shut and stays shut at a certain voltage). Normally, the inactivation lock clicks shut around -55 mV. This drug **tightens that inactivation lock** so it clicks shut earlier — at **-65 mV** instead.

Now your resting membrane potential is -70 mV. Before the drug, the door was ready to spring open when you reached -55 mV. After the drug, at -70 mV, the inactivation lock is **already clicked shut**. The door is **deadbolted** before you even knock.

Threshold doesn't move. You still need -55 mV to turn the activation handle. But the door won't budge because the inactivation lock is already engaged. The cell is **refractory** — harder to excite because the channels are **pre-inactivated** at rest. That is the **use-dependent block** in ischemic tissue: more channels start in the deadbolted state, so fewer are available to fire.

Let me reset this for you. Forget the threshold number.

The drug does **not** change the threshold. Threshold stays at **-55 mV**. What changes is the **voltage at which the inactivation gate slams shut**.

Think of a mousetrap. The trap arm (activation gate) snaps when you touch the cheese at -55 mV. But there is also a **safety latch** (inactivation gate) that can lock the arm down before you even reach for the cheese. Normally the safety latch only engages at -55 mV too. This drug makes the safety latch engage earlier — at **-65 mV**.

So at resting potential of -70 mV, the safety latch is **already engaged**. The trap is **locked** before you even start moving toward the cheese. You still need to reach -55 mV to spring the trap, but the trap **cannot spring** because the safety latch is holding it down.

That is **inactivation**: the channel is present but unavailable. More channels start unavailable at rest. That is the **use-dependent block** in ischemic tissue.
